Explain what the following Python function `pdb_on_exception` does and how it works.

```python
# repository: boltons, file: boltons/debugutils.py
import sys
import time
from reprlib import Repr

def pdb_on_exception(limit=100):
    """Installs a handler which, instead of exiting, attaches a
    post-mortem pdb console whenever an unhandled exception is
    encountered.

    Args:
        limit (int): the max number of stack frames to display when
            printing the traceback

    A similar effect can be achieved from the command-line using the
    following command::

      python -m pdb your_code.py

    But ``pdb_on_exception`` allows you to do this conditionally and within
    your application. To restore default behavior, just do::

      sys.excepthook = sys.__excepthook__
    """
    import pdb
    import sys
    import traceback

    def pdb_excepthook(exc_type, exc_val, exc_tb):
        traceback.print_tb(exc_tb, limit=limit)
        pdb.post_mortem(exc_tb)

    sys.excepthook = pdb_excepthook
    return
```
response: The `pdb_on_exception` function from the boltons library sets up a custom exception handler that uses Python's debugger (PDB) to provide an interactive debugging session whenever an unhandled exception occurs in your code. It takes one optional argument, `limit`, which specifies the maximum number of stack frames to display when printing the traceback before entering the PDB console. By replacing the default system-wide excepthook with this custom function, any uncaught exceptions will trigger a post-mortem debugging session instead of terminating the program abruptly. This allows developers to inspect the state of their application at the point where an exception was raised and understand what led up to it. To revert back to the original behavior, you can simply reset `sys.excepthook` to its default value using `sys.__excepthook__`.
